theme: Arrest; trials before the Sanhedrin and Pilate
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 26:47-27:31. Jesus is arrested, tried by the Sanhedrin, denied by Peter, handed over to Pilate, and mocked by soldiers. Watch how Jesus responds to each trial, and contrast his behavior with that of Peter and Judas.
settingTheScene: It is the night and early morning of Good Friday. Jesus is arrested in the garden by a crowd sent by the chief priests, led by Judas. He is taken to the high priest Caiaphas, where he is tried at night. At dawn he is delivered to the Roman governor Pilate, because only Rome could carry out a death sentence. The man who had healed and taught is now abandoned, mocked, and condemned.
observation: “Friend, do what you came to do” (26:50).
“Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword” (26:52).
“Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (26:53).
“I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God” (26:63).
“You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power” (26:64).
“And he went out and wept bitterly” (26:75).
“I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (27:4).
“His blood be on us and on our children” (27:25).
interpretation:
Everything in the arrest shows that Jesus is in control. He tells Peter to put away his sword. He could call twelve legions of angels, but then the Scriptures could not be fulfilled. He goes willingly. All the disciples flee.

Before the Sanhedrin, the trial is a sham. False witnesses cannot agree. Finally the high priest asks under oath if he is the Christ. Jesus answers by combining Psalm 110 and Daniel 7: he will be seen seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven. The high priest tears his robes and declares blasphemy. The council spits on him and strikes him. Jesus is condemned for telling the truth about who he is.

Meanwhile, Peter denies him three times as Jesus predicted, and when the rooster crows, he goes out and weeps bitterly. Judas, too, is filled with remorse and returns the silver, saying, “I have sinned.” But he goes and hangs himself. The difference between Peter and Judas is not in their sin but where they turned. Peter would later be restored. Judas despaired. True repentance turns to Christ and is met by his mercy.

Before Pilate, Jesus is silent when accused. Pilate knows that the leaders delivered him up out of envy. His wife sends a message: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man.” Pilate offers to release Barabbas or Jesus. The crowd chooses Barabbas, a criminal. The innocent one takes the guilty man’s place. Pilate washes his hands and has Jesus flogged. The soldiers mock him with a scarlet robe, a crown of thorns, and a reed scepter, and kneel to him in mockery. They did not know they were saying the truth: here is the King.
connection: Isaiah 53:7 says “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter… he opened not his mouth.” Psalm 22:7-8 describes the mocking. Daniel 7:13-14 and Psalm 110:1 stand behind Jesus’ answer. 1 Peter 2:21-24 says Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example. 2 Corinthians 5:21: for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin. Luke 22:61-62 adds that the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Galatians 3:13. Hebrews 12:2-3.
application:
Place yourself in Peter’s sandals. Where have you denied Jesus by silence or by fear? Bring it to him, and know that he restores.

Consider Barabbas: Jesus took the place of a guilty man. You are Barabbas. Let that humble and move you.

Notice the silence of Jesus before his accusers, and ask the Spirit to give you patience when you are misjudged.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for going willingly to be arrested for you.
Confess where you have denied him.
